section.title: Preach the Word
section.sectionRationale: The letter reaches its charge. Before God and Christ the Judge, Paul solemnly commands Timothy to preach the word, ready in season and out, precisely because a time is coming when people will not endure sound doctrine but will gather teachers to suit their own desires. Then Paul turns to himself: already being poured out like a drink offering, he looks back on a finished race and forward to the crown of righteousness, held not for him alone but for all who love Christ's appearing.
section.thesis: In view of Christ's coming judgment and kingdom, Timothy must preach the word faithfully in every season, even as people turn from sound doctrine to myths; for Paul, poured out and near departure, has fought the good fight and kept the faith, and the righteous Judge will award the crown to all who love His appearing.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the solemn charge to preach the word in season and out of season; the warning that people will not endure sound doctrine, so Timothy must fulfill his ministry; and Paul poured out like a drink offering, finishing the race and awaiting the crown of righteousness.

verses.text: I {{diamartyromai|charge}} you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His {{epiphaneia|appearing}} and His kingdom:
{{kerysso|Preach}} the word; be prepared {{eukairos_akairos|in season and out of season}}; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction.
For the time will come when men will not tolerate {{hygiaino|sound}} doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires.
So they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths.
But you, be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.

units.label: Poured out, finishing well
units.note: the good fight, the crown of righteousness

verses.text: For I am already being {{spendo|poured out}} like a drink offering, and the time of my {{analysis|departure}} is at hand.
I have fought the {{agon|good fight}}, I have finished the {{dromos|race}}, I have kept the faith.

From now on there is laid up for me the {{stephanos|crown}} of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing.

diamartyromai.gloss: To charge solemnly, to testify earnestly, to adjure as before a witness. Paul does not merely advise Timothy; he places him under oath in the presence of God and of Christ the Judge. The weight of the command comes from the One before whom it is given, so preaching the word is not one option among many but a sacred duty owed to God.

epiphaneia.gloss: A shining forth, an appearing, used for the visible coming of Christ in glory. The charge is framed by His appearing and His kingdom, so all ministry is done in the light of Christ's return and reign. The same appearing that Timothy is to serve is the appearing that Paul, at the end, longs for and loves.

kerysso.gloss: To herald, to proclaim publicly as an official messenger. A herald does not invent his message but announces the word given by his king. So Timothy is to preach the word, not his own opinions, delivering God's message with the authority of the One who sent him and adding nothing and subtracting nothing.

eukairos_akairos.gloss: In season and out of season, when it is convenient and when it is not. The paired adverbs press the herald to constant readiness: he does not wait for a welcome or a favorable mood but stands prepared at every moment. Faithfulness in preaching is measured not by the audience's appetite but by the messenger's readiness.

hygiaino.gloss: To be healthy, sound, in good health; the root of our word hygiene. Sound doctrine is healthy teaching that produces spiritual health, in contrast to teaching that corrupts. The tragedy Paul foresees is people rejecting what heals them in favor of what merely flatters, choosing sickness because it suits their desires.

spendo.gloss: To be poured out as a drink offering, a libation poured beside a sacrifice. Paul sees his coming death as an act of worship: his life's blood poured out to God like the wine poured over an altar. His martyrdom is not defeat but offering, the fitting end of a life already given wholly to Christ.

analysis.gloss: A loosing, an unbinding, a departure; the word for casting off a ship's moorings or striking camp to set out. Paul does not speak of dying so much as of departing, of being released to go home. Death for the believer is the loosing of ropes for a voyage to the Lord, not an end but a setting out.

agon.gloss: A contest, struggle, or fight, drawn from the athletic games and the battlefield. The Christian life is no gentle stroll but a strenuous contest that demands everything. Paul does not say he won by his own strength but that he fought the good fight, the noble contest worth all its cost, staying in it to the end.

dromos.gloss: A course, a running track, the race set before a runner. Paul pictures his ministry as a marked-out course now completed, not abandoned partway. To finish the race is to persevere to the appointed end, and the joy is not in speed or applause but in having run the whole distance God assigned.

stephanos.gloss: A crown, the victor's wreath awarded to the winner of the games, not a royal diadem. The crown of righteousness is the reward of grace given by the righteous Judge, laid up and certain. It is promised not to Paul alone but to all who love Christ's appearing, so the finish line and its crown belong to every faithful believer.

basic.context: Having grounded Timothy in the God-breathed Scriptures, Paul now issues the charge the whole letter has been building toward. He commands Timothy, as if under oath before God and Christ the Judge, to preach the word at all times, whether it is welcomed or not. He warns that people will increasingly refuse healthy teaching and collect teachers who tell them what they want to hear. Against that tide Timothy must keep a clear head, bear hardship, and finish his ministry. Then Paul speaks of himself: his death is near, his life is being poured out like an offering, but he has stayed faithful to the end and a crown awaits him and everyone who loves Christ's return.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a direct charge to a pastor, yet its truths reach the whole church. Preaching God's word faithfully, whether or not it is popular, is the God-appointed means of guarding the flock. The warning about itching ears is a permanent danger, not a one-time event. And Paul's confidence at death models the hope held out to every believer who keeps the faith.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul solemnly charges, diamartyromai, Timothy in view of Christ's epiphaneia, His appearing. He is to kerysso, to herald, the word eukairos akairos, in season and out of season, because people will refuse hygiaino teaching, sound and healthy doctrine. Paul is being spendo, poured out like a drink offering, near his analysis, his departure. He has fought the agon, the good fight, finished the dromos, the race, and awaits the stephanos, the victor's crown.
basic.typology: The drink offering poured beside the sacrifices of Israel is fulfilled as Paul pours out his life to God. The victor's crown of the games becomes the crown of righteousness given by the righteous Judge to all who finish faithful.
basic.christ: Christ is the Judge of the living and the dead, the King whose appearing and kingdom frame the whole charge. He is the righteous Judge who awards the crown, and the One whose appearing believers are to love. The word Timothy preaches is the message of Christ, and the faith Paul kept is faith in Him.
basic.god: God, before whom the charge is given, will judge all people through Christ. He is the God to whom Paul's life is poured out as an offering, and the faithful Judge who has laid up a sure reward. He is worthy of a ministry that does not bend to the crowd but holds to His word to the end.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 2 speaks of Paul being poured out as a drink offering on the sacrifice of their faith. First Corinthians 9 pictures the Christian life as a race run for an imperishable crown. Second Timothy 3 grounds this charge in the God-breathed Scriptures Timothy is to preach.
basic.oneStory: God has always advanced His purposes by His word carried on faithful lips, from prophets to apostles to preachers like Timothy. Paul, at the end of his course, hands the word on and pours out his life, confident that the same word will run on after him. The story moves toward Christ's appearing, when the righteous Judge will crown all who kept the faith and loved His coming.

context.literary:
The passage is a single sweep with three movements, and the hinge words are the little "but you" of verse 5 and the "for I" of verse 6. In verses 1 to 2 Paul gives a charge in the formal manner of a legal oath, naming the witnesses and the Judge, and then fires off five imperatives in a row: preach, be prepared, reprove, rebuke, encourage. Verses 3 and 4 give the reason in a prophecy of refusal, and verse 5 turns back to Timothy with four more commands: be sober, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry. The pairing of "you" and "they" runs the length of the section. They will gather teachers to suit their desires; but you.

Verses 6 to 8 are the personal counterpart. The "for" in verse 6 makes Paul's coming death the ground of the whole charge: because his own course is almost run, Timothy must take up the baton. The three clauses of verse 7 are tidy and balanced, each a short perfect-tense statement of the form "I have ...", with an image from the arena (the fight), the track (the race) and the trust (the faith). Verse 8 then looks forward, and the movement from past to future is plain: I have fought, finished, kept; now laid up for me is a crown.

The passage also holds an inclusio of Christ's appearing. The charge begins "in view of His appearing and His kingdom" and the crown is given to "all who crave His appearing." The whole of the ministry, from preaching to dying, is held between the two mentions. Everything between is lived in the light of the day when the Judge appears.

It is the emotional peak of the letter. The earlier chapters teach and exhort; here Paul speaks as a man who has nothing left to prove and nothing left to hide, and the tone moves from urgency to calm in the space of eight verses.
context.historical:
Paul writes from a Roman jail, probably during a second imprisonment under Nero, in the mid or late 60s. The letter says that he had already had a first hearing, 4:16, and that he now expects to die, 4:6. Church tradition holds that Paul was executed in Rome, and the text of this letter fits that, though the letter itself does not report his death.

The oath-like opening would have sounded very much like a courtroom formula. A person might be solemnly charged before witnesses; Paul places Timothy before God and Christ as the witnesses and, in the same breath, as the Judge. "The living and the dead" is a standard phrase in the apostolic preaching, Acts 10:42 and 1 Peter 4:5, for the universality of the coming judgment. For people who were living under the arbitrary and sometimes deadly rule of a Roman emperor, that was a quiet claim that the final court is not at Rome.

The warning about itching ears is rooted in the real situation of the churches around Ephesus. In the ancient world, itinerant teachers and orators moved from city to city offering their wares, and they lived on the goodwill of their audiences. A teacher who flattered did well, and one who corrected did not. The church was never free from the temptation to prefer a pleasing speaker, and Paul had said much the same to the Ephesian elders years before, Acts 20:29-30.

Paul's picture of a drink offering belongs to the sacrificial system of Israel and the wider ancient world. In Israel, wine was poured out beside the burnt offering and the grain offering, Numbers 15:5 and 28:7, as a final act of worship. The athletic images, the contest, the race and the crown, would have been familiar in any Greek city, where games were a normal part of civic life, and Paul used them elsewhere, 1 Corinthians 9:24-27. A victor's wreath was awarded by the judge at the end, not by the crowd, and that is why he calls the Lord the "righteous Judge."
context.canonical:
The command to preach the word has a long canonical root. Moses charged Israel to teach God's words diligently, Deuteronomy 6:7, and the prophets were sent to speak whether people listened or not, Ezekiel 2:4-5. Jeremiah was told to stand and speak all that he was commanded, Jeremiah 1:17. Paul's phrase "in season and out of season" resembles the character of the prophetic task: the message is given regardless of the mood of the hearers.

The itching-ears warning belongs to a line of passages about people who wanted a pleasing message. Isaiah heard Israel say to the seers, "Do not see," and to the prophets, "Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us pleasant things," Isaiah 30:10. Jeremiah complained of prophets who said "Peace, peace" when there was no peace, Jeremiah 6:14. The pattern is old and Paul expects it to continue.

Paul's own words in Acts 20:27-31 are the nearest parallel: he did not shrink back from declaring the whole will of God, and he warned that wolves would come from the very number of the elders. The apostolic generation had a consistent expectation that fidelity to the word would be tested.

The drink offering of verse 6 links to Philippians 2:17, where Paul uses the same picture of himself being poured out on the sacrifice and service of the Philippians' faith, and to the sacrificial pattern of Numbers 28. The fight, the race and the crown recall 1 Corinthians 9:24-27, Hebrews 12:1 and 1 Timothy 6:12. The crown is promised elsewhere to elders in 1 Peter 5:4 and to the faithful in James 1:12 and Revelation 2:10.

The last line, "all who crave His appearing," ties the passage to the New Testament's hope. Titus 2:13 speaks of the blessed hope and the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, and Hebrews 9:28 says that Christ will appear a second time to bring salvation to those waiting for Him.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to keep a younger man on his feet at a time of grief and danger. The charge says three things. First, who is watching: God and Christ, who will judge. Timothy is to preach not because the crowd demands it, nor because he is at ease, but because he must give account. Second, what to do: bring the word, in every circumstance, using every means the word itself provides, reproof, rebuke and encouragement, and keep doing it patiently. Third, what to expect: people will get tired of sound teaching and look for teachers who will say what they want to hear.

The second movement is meant to inoculate Timothy against discouragement. He is told ahead of time that refusal is coming, so that he is not thrown when it arrives. The charge is not conditional on success. The way Paul phrases verse 5 shows what Timothy needs most: a clear head, willingness to suffer, and a refusal to leave the work unfinished.

The last paragraph is the example. Paul wants Timothy to see what it looks like at the end of a faithful life. It is not an advertisement for Paul but a promise for Timothy: if you do what I have done, you will have what I have. And the crown is not only for the apostle, but for everyone who longs for Christ's appearing, so a listener who wondered whether a crown was reserved for great men would learn that it is for all who love Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this passage is direct command to a particular pastor: preach, reprove, rebuke, encourage, do the work of an evangelist. These imperatives belong first to Timothy's office, yet the New Testament does not limit the task of speaking the word to people with a title. Believers are told to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly and to teach and admonish one another, Colossians 3:16, and the church shares in the work of making the gospel known. So the principle carries to every Christian, while the particular charge to preach in the assembly belongs to those whom the church sets apart for it.

The prophecy about the time that is coming is description, but it carries a warning and an implied command. The church is not told to set a date, nor to treat all unpopularity as proof of faithfulness; it is told to stay with sound doctrine. Not every preacher who is disliked is right, and Paul's own list of means, with its call for patient instruction, rules out harshness for its own sake.

Verses 6 to 8 describe Paul's own end. They do not prescribe that every believer will die a martyr or that every life will feel finished. They do offer a picture of confidence that is open to all who keep the faith, and a promise that the crown is for every one who loves the Lord's appearing, not for apostles alone.

debates.question: Who are the people with itching ears in verses 3 and 4?

views.label: Professing believers within the church
views.case: Paul says they will 'gather around themselves teachers,' which assumes a congregation with teachers to choose from. They are people who still want religion, but religion shaped to their desires. The warning in Acts 20:30 about men rising up from the elders' own number is of the same kind.

views.label: Unbelievers who reject the gospel
views.case: The language of refusing sound doctrine and turning to myths can describe people outside the faith who have never held it. On this reading the verse speaks of the wider culture's appetite for pleasing messages, and Timothy's task is to go on proclaiming to people who will not listen.

debates.bearing: The context favors the first view, for Timothy is a pastor and the teachers are being 'gathered' by people who want them. Yet the warning also reaches outward. Wherever people choose a message for its comfort and not its truth, the same appetite is at work.

debates.question: What is the 'crown of righteousness' in verse 8?

views.label: A reward given for a righteous life
views.case: The crown is 'awarded' by the Judge, the language of recompense, and the athletic setting suggests a prize for completing the course. Paul's three claims in verse 7 seem to be the grounds on which it is given.

views.label: The righteousness itself, the final verdict and state of the believer
views.case: The phrase can mean a crown that consists of righteousness, the completed verdict of acquittal and the perfect holiness to come. On this reading the crown is the blessing of being declared right with God, the same righteousness by faith that Paul preaches, Romans 3:22 and Philippians 3:9, brought to fulfilment on the last day.

debates.bearing: Paul says the Lord 'will award' the crown as a righteous Judge, and he says it is for 'all who crave His appearing,' not for the most accomplished. Whatever the exact sense, the crown is not wages earned from God, which Romans 4:4-5 would not allow. It is the gift of the Judge to those who belong to Him, and faithfulness is the evidence of that love, not its purchase price.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 opens with diamartyromai, to testify solemnly, to call witnesses and charge under oath. Paul uses it elsewhere of testifying to the gospel of God's grace in Acts 20:24. Here the word has a courtroom ring, and the unusual feature is that the witnesses and the Judge are the same persons. The charge is given in the presence of God and Christ, and then Christ is named as the one who will judge.

The verb for "preach" in verse 2 is kerysso, the herald's word. A kerux in the ancient world was a messenger who proclaimed a king's decree in public and did not alter it. The point is that the word is delivered, not edited. In the same verse "be prepared" is the verb ephistemi, to stand by or be at hand. It suggests readiness as a standing posture, not an occasional effort. The paired adverbs "in season and out of season" set the convenient against the inconvenient. The next three verbs form a progression: reprove, which brings a fault to light, rebuke, which presses it home, and encourage, parakaleo, the word that means both to exhort and to comfort. The three are bound together by "every form of patient instruction," makrothymia and didache, long-suffering and teaching, so that correction is always joined to patience and to substance.

In verse 3 "sound" translates hygiaino, which gives us the word hygiene. It is Paul's favorite adjective for teaching in the pastoral letters, as in 1 Timothy 1:10 and Titus 1:9, and it means healthy, life-giving. The picture of "itching ears" comes from a Greek verb that means to scratch or tickle, so the hearers are literally ears in need of a scratch, and they hire teachers who will provide it. In verse 4 the ears are turned away from the truth and turned aside to myths, the same two verbs in the active sense of turning away and turning aside. The ear is the organ of decision here: where it is turned shows what a person is after.

Verse 5 begins with nepho, to be sober, the opposite of drunkenness, and it means clear-headed and watchful. Kakopatheo, "endure hardship," is the same verb Paul used in 2:9, and he again asks Timothy to be willing to suffer. The word euangelistes, evangelist, is rare, appearing also in Acts 21:8 and Ephesians 4:11, and it names a gospel-bringer, not an office with specified powers.

In verse 6 the verb spendo, "poured out," is used for a drink offering poured at an altar, and its passive form, "I am being poured out," pictures Paul as the wine being poured. "Departure," analysis, is related to the verb analyo that Paul used in Philippians 1:23 when he said he had the desire to depart and be with Christ. The picture is often explained as the loosing of a ship's moorings or the breaking of a tent, an image of release, not of loss.

In verse 7 each of the three clauses is in the perfect tense: I have fought, I have finished, I have kept. The perfect tense speaks of an action completed whose result stands. The agon is the contest, and the adjective "good" (kalos) is the same as in 1 Timothy 6:12, where Timothy is told to fight the good fight. "Kept the faith" uses the verb tereo, to guard, which links back to the good deposit of 1:14 that Timothy was to guard.

In verse 8 stephanos is the victor's wreath, as distinct from diadema, a royal crown. "Laid up" (apokeitai) means stored in reserve, and "awarded" is the verb apodidomi, to hand over what is due or owed. The verb behind "crave" is agapao in the perfect tense: those who have loved and still love His appearing.

typology.type: The drink offering poured out, 2 Timothy 4:6
typology.fulfillment: In Israel's worship, wine was poured out at the altar beside the burnt offering and the grain offering, Numbers 15:5-10 and 28:7, as the last, costly act of devotion. Paul uses that picture of his own life, as he did earlier of the Philippians' service in Philippians 2:17. The correspondence is that a life is given to God as an act of worship. The escalation is in Christ, whose life was poured out unto death for many, Isaiah 53:12 and Mark 14:24, and whose sacrifice is the only one that takes away sin, Hebrews 10:12. Paul's pouring out is not atonement, only participation in the service of the one sacrifice.

typology.type: The race and the crown of the games, 2 Timothy 4:7-8
typology.fulfillment: The Greek games gave a wreath to the winner who kept the rules, a perishable crown, 1 Corinthians 9:25. Paul takes the picture and turns it. The prize is imperishable, the Judge is righteous, and the crown is offered not to a single winner but to everyone who loves His appearing. Christ has already run the race set before Him, Hebrews 12:1-2, and finished the work He was given, John 17:4, and so believers run with their eyes on Him, not to earn a place but to follow Him home. The type falls short in that games produce one winner among many, whereas in Christ all who finish share the crown.

typology.type: The solemn charge before witnesses, 2 Timothy 4:1
typology.fulfillment: The charge before God and the Judge recalls Israel's covenant ceremonies, in which witnesses were called to hold the people to the Lord's word, Deuteronomy 30:19 and 31:28. Timothy stands in that tradition as a messenger who must give account. The escalation is that the Judge is now known by name and by face: Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, Acts 17:31. The covenant lawsuit of the prophets finds its climax in one person, and the faithful messenger can speak without fear, because the Judge is also the Saviour who laid down His life for the people he will judge.

study.christ:
The charge is given in the presence of Christ and in view of His appearing, and the passage cannot be read without Him. He is the one before whom Timothy stands, the Judge of the living and the dead, and the King whose kingdom is coming. The whole of Timothy's work is set under His eyes. This is not an abstract threat: the Judge is the Lord who loved His servants and gave Himself for them, and so the shadow of judgment falls on the preacher as the shadow of a master who is also a friend.

The content of what Timothy is to preach is the word, and that word is, in the end, a person. In the pastoral letters the "word" and the "gospel" are one message, the good news that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, 1 Timothy 1:15. When Timothy heralds the word, he heralds the Christ of whom the Scriptures speak, as the previous passage said. And the sound teaching that people will not endure is described in 1 Timothy 6:3 as "the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ." Refusing it is, in the end, refusing Him.

Paul's life is poured out in Christ's pattern. Jesus said at the Last Supper that His blood was poured out for many, Matthew 26:28, and the apostle's own life is described in terms that echo the offerings of the old order. What Paul gives is not a sacrifice for sin, but it is a sacrifice of service shaped by the one sacrifice. He follows a Lord who finished the work given to Him, as John 17:4 and the cry of John 19:30 declare. The "I have finished" of verse 7 is the apostle's small echo of the Lord's great "It is finished."

Christ is also the Judge who awards the crown, and the title "righteous Judge" is a deliberate comfort. The one who will examine every life has already borne judgment for His own, Romans 8:1 and 8:34. So Paul can speak of the day with joy, because the verdict he awaits is the one declared by the one who died for him. The crown is for those who love His appearing, which is love for Him, not merely for the reward.

As a caution, the passage does not make Paul himself the pattern of salvation. The crown is given on the ground of the righteousness that comes through Christ, and the strength for the fight came from Him, 4:17. The connection to Christ is not that Paul replaces Him, but that the apostle's finished course is a gift from the one who finished first.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the God who judges, and the judgment is described as an assurance and a warning together. The charge is given before Him and before Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, so no one, whether a pastor, a hearer or an emperor, is outside His court. The passage teaches that God sees the work of His servants and that nothing is hidden before Him. That doctrine is both searching and consoling: it searches the preacher who is tempted to flatter, and it consoles the one who labors where no one notices.

God is also the God who has spoken. Timothy is to preach "the word," and the demand for faithfulness rests on the fact that this word is not the preacher's own. The previous passage said Scripture is God-breathed; this one says it is to be heralded. A God who has spoken is a God who may be known, and a word from Him is not to be adjusted to what the audience prefers. Those who gather teachers to suit their desires are, in the end, trying to construct a god who will tell them what they want to hear. The God of Scripture is not that. He tells the truth and calls it healthy.

He is righteous. The title "righteous Judge" is the center of verse 8. His justice is not arbitrary or cruel, and His verdicts can be trusted, in contrast with the unjust courts under which Paul was tried. Because He is righteous, those who have suffered injustice can wait with confidence. Because He is also gracious, the same Judge gives a crown to people who deserved nothing.

He is faithful to those who finish. In verse 8 the crown is "laid up," stored in reserve, which suggests that the reward is already prepared and waiting, as the hope in Colossians 1:5 is laid up in heaven. God does not leave the end of a servant's life to chance. The one who began a good work will bring it to completion, Philippians 1:6.

There is a tension between the severity and the tenderness. The same passage speaks of coming judgment and of a crown for all who love His appearing, of hard times and of settled peace. The tension is resolved in the fact that the Judge is the Saviour. He does not wait for the day of appearing to show His love; He has already given Himself, Titus 2:14.

For worship, the passage draws us into a stance of watchfulness and longing. To love His appearing is to pray as the church has prayed, "Come, Lord Jesus," and to serve now in the light of that day, with a clear head, a willing back and a steady voice.

crossReferences.note: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders. He says he never shrank from declaring the whole will of God and warns that wolves will come, even from among them, to distort the truth. It is the earlier form of the warning in verses 3 and 4 and shows that Timothy's situation was foreseen years before.

Paul says that even if he is being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of the Philippians' faith, he is glad and rejoices with them all. It is the first appearance of the picture used in verse 6, and there, from a prison, it carries joy where here it carries calm.

The law of the daily offering, in which a quarter hin of fermented drink was poured out to the LORD in the sanctuary area beside each lamb. It supplies the background of the drink offering image and shows that such pouring was an ordinary and honorable part of worship, not a loss.

Paul's earlier use of the athlete's picture: all run but one receives the prize, and the runner trains with discipline for a perishable crown while believers compete for an imperishable one. It gives the background to the race and crown of verses 7 and 8, and shows the same mind at work years before.

Timothy was told, 'Fight the good fight of the faith.' Paul now says that he has himself fought the good fight. The echo turns the instruction into an example, so that the charge to Timothy and the report of Paul are two ends of the same road.

The great cloud of witnesses and the call to run with endurance the race set out for us. Paul's finished course joins that cloud, and the verse helps readers see that the race is run in the company of those who ran before, with the eyes fixed on Jesus, as the next verse says.

When the Chief Shepherd appears, elders will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away. It is a parallel promise for those who shepherd God's flock, and it shows that the crown of 2 Timothy 4:8 is not a peculiar privilege of the apostle.

The grace of God has appeared, and believers wait for the blessed hope and glorious appearance of Jesus. The passage joins the past appearing and the future one, and it explains why loving His appearing goes with a life of good works and renounced ungodliness.

Peter says that Jesus commanded the apostles to preach and to testify that He is the one appointed by God as Judge of the living and the dead. It is the source of Paul's phrase in verse 1 and shows that the charge to preach and the announcement of the Judge belong together.

The people tell the seers not to see and the prophets not to prophesy what is right, but to speak pleasant things. It is the Old Testament counterpart of the itching ears, and shows that wanting a flattering message is an old and persistent temptation, not a new one.

The hope laid up for believers in heaven, the same word used for the crown laid up in verse 8. The link shows that what is stored in reserve is the hope itself, and that the believer's confidence rests on what God keeps, not on what a person achieves.

study.oneStory:
From the start, the Bible has a pattern of one messenger after another carrying God's word to a people who do not much want it. Noah preached, Moses spoke to Pharaoh and to Israel, the prophets stood before kings who preferred their court prophets, and John the Baptist cried in the wilderness. The ministry Paul hands to Timothy is a continuation of that long line. The people who gather teachers to suit their desires are the heirs of those who said to the seers, "Do not see," and of the Israelites who wanted a king like the nations. The itching ears are as old as Eden, where the question "Did God really say?" was the first sermon in a hostile key.

Paul's charge also places the preacher in the story of redemption, at the point between the first appearing of Christ and the second. The word is heralded now because the King has come and is coming. The preaching of the word is the means by which a people for Himself is gathered, the way the nations hear and are brought in, as Paul says in 4:17. The task is not to improve the world by advice but to announce a king.

The passage looks back at the sacrificial system and forward to the day of judgment. The drink offering poured at the altar stands for all the offerings that pointed to Christ, and Paul's life, poured out in union with His, is a small part of that unfolding. The race run and finished, the faith kept and the fight fought are the long obedience of those who trust Him. Their end is to receive a crown from the Judge, who is also their Saviour.

In the new creation the crown is shown to be a gift that leads to worship. Revelation 4:10 pictures the elders casting their crowns before the throne, and the image fits what Paul has said. The crown is real, but it is laid down in praise. The "appearing" which the faithful crave is finally the day when the Lord comes, when every enemy is put down, when the word of God that was heralded in a hostile world is seen to have been true, and when the one who judged and saved is seen face to face. The preaching ends in sight.

sermon.title: Preach the Word
sermon.why: Part of Begg's series A Study in 2 Timothy, this message expounds the solemn charge of 2 Timothy 4:1-2, unfolding what it means to preach the word in season and out of season before God and Christ the Judge, and why faithful proclamation is the church's abiding duty.

quiz.q: On what basis does Paul issue his charge to preach the word?

options.text: In the presence of God and Christ the Judge, in view of His appearing and kingdom.
options.note: Verse 1 grounds the charge in God's presence and Christ's coming judgment and reign.

options.text: On the strength of Paul's own personal authority alone.
options.note: Paul writes with apostolic authority, but the charge is grounded in God and Christ the Judge, not himself.

options.text: Because preaching was culturally respected in that day.
options.note: Paul warns the culture will reject sound teaching; the ground is God, not popularity.

options.text: Because ministry is done before God and in light of Christ's return.
options.note: True and close, restating the coming appearing and kingdom that frame the charge.

quiz.q: What does in season and out of season require of Timothy?

options.text: Constant readiness to preach whether it is welcome or not.
options.note: The paired words press unwavering readiness in every circumstance.

options.text: Preaching only when the audience is eager to listen.
options.note: The opposite: he must preach even when it is unwelcome.

options.text: Preaching only during the appointed seasons of the year.
options.note: It is about readiness at all times, not the calendar.

options.text: Faithfulness that does not depend on the crowd's appetite.
options.note: True and close, capturing the readiness that ignores convenience.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say a time is coming when people will not tolerate sound doctrine?

options.text: Because with itching ears they will gather teachers to suit their own desires.
options.note: Verses 3 and 4 name itching ears and self-chosen teachers turning to myths.

options.text: Because sound doctrine will no longer exist to be preached.
options.note: The word remains; the problem is people refusing it.

options.text: Because all teachers will have abandoned the truth entirely.
options.note: The issue is hearers collecting agreeable teachers, not the total loss of faithful ones.

options.text: Because people will prefer teaching that flatters their desires.
options.note: True and close, summarizing the itching ears that reject healthy doctrine.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe his approaching death?

options.text: As being poured out like a drink offering, the time of his departure at hand.
options.note: Verse 6 uses the drink offering and departure to picture death as worship and release.

options.text: As a tragic and meaningless end to his work.
options.note: Paul sees it as offering and departure, full of hope, not meaningless.

options.text: As proof that his ministry had finally failed.
options.note: He speaks of a finished race and a crown, not failure.

options.text: As a life offered to God and a release to go home.
options.note: True and close, drawing out the offering and the departure imagery.

quiz.q: To whom is the crown of righteousness promised?

options.text: To Paul and to all who love Christ's appearing.
options.note: Verse 8 extends the crown beyond Paul to all who long for Christ's coming.

options.text: To Paul alone, as a unique apostle.
options.note: Paul explicitly says not only to me but to all who love His appearing.

options.text: To those who earn it by outdoing others in good works.
options.note: The crown is grace from the righteous Judge, not a reward for outperforming others.

options.text: To every believer who keeps the faith and longs for His return.
options.note: True and close, restating the promise to all who love His appearing.

questions: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ the Judge. How would remembering that you live and serve in God's presence change the way you speak and act this week?
Faithful preaching means the word in season and out of season, welcome or not. Where are you tempted to soften or stay silent about God's truth because it is unpopular?
Itching ears gather teachers who confirm what they already want. What voices are you drawn to, and are they feeding you healthy doctrine or simply flattering your desires?
Paul faced death as a life poured out and a departure to be with the Lord. How does his hope reshape the way you think about your own death and what you are living for now?
The crown of righteousness is promised to all who love Christ's appearing. Do you long for His return, and how would loving His appearing change your priorities today?

translationNotes.note: In season and out of season renders two paired adverbs pressing constant readiness, whether the moment is convenient or not.
Poured out like a drink offering echoes the libation poured beside Israel's sacrifices; departure translates a word for loosing a ship's moorings or striking a tent.
Crown here is the victor's wreath of the games, not a royal diadem.
